For three weeks of the summer I turned sixteen, I answered the telephone at WKLM, a community radio station that broadcasts from two rooms above a dry cleaner on Water Street. The station was on the air twenty-four hours a day, which meant that somebody had to sit in the booth from midnight to six, and that somebody was usually Mr. Bello.

Mr. Bello was seventy-one and had hosted the overnight show for nineteen years. He played jazz records from his own collection, which he carried up the stairs in two milk crates every evening, and between songs he talked to his listeners as if each of them were sitting across a kitchen table. He knew most of them by name: the baker who started work at three, the nurse driving home from the hospital, a long-haul trucker who called every Thursday from somewhere new.

My job was to screen calls and keep the coffee coming. Around the second week, I noticed that Mr. Bello kept a spiral notebook beside the microphone, and that in it he wrote down every caller's name along with whatever they had mentioned the last time: a daughter's wedding, a sick dog, a promotion they were hoping for. When the trucker called, Mr. Bello asked whether he had finally made it to the Grand Canyon. He had. It was the kindest piece of bookkeeping I have ever seen.

On my last Friday, Mr. Bello's voice gave out halfway through the night. He coughed, waved me toward the microphone, and wrote on a napkin: "Just talk to them." I sat down in his chair with my heart pounding. For the first ten minutes I read the weather twice and introduced the same record two times in a row. Then the telephone lit up. It was the nurse, asking where Mr. Bello was.

I told her the truth: that he had lost his voice and that I was the summer help. There was a pause, and then she said she hoped he would drink some tea with honey, and asked me what I was going to study in college. Somehow that question loosened something. I told her about the biology class I was dreading and the cross-country team I was hoping to make, and when I looked at the clock, twenty minutes had gone by.

Mr. Bello had been listening from the couch in the back room. When I came off the air at six, he handed me the spiral notebook, open to a fresh page. At the top, in his careful capital letters, he had written the nurse's name, and under it: "Biology, dreading. Cross-country, hoping."

I still have that page. I keep it in the front of whatever notebook I happen to be using, and when I have to speak to a room full of strangers, I look at it first.

My parents spoke Vietnamese at home until I was eight, and then, without anyone deciding it, they stopped. I had begun answering them in English, first out of laziness and then on purpose, because a girl at school had laughed when my mother called to me across the playground. By the time I was ten, the language of our dinner table had changed, and my parents' sentences had grown shorter.

My grandmother, who lived with us, never made the switch. She would ask me questions at dinner, and I would answer with a shrug or a single English word, and my father would translate for me in a low voice, as if I were a guest. Eventually she stopped asking. She spent her evenings on the telephone with her sister in Da Nang instead, laughing in a way I rarely heard at our table.

At the time this seemed like a fair trade. I was fluent in the things that mattered to me then: the slang of the school bus, the rules of the games we played at recess, the lyrics of every song on the radio. Vietnamese belonged to holidays and to the long, puzzling phone calls my parents made late at night when somebody overseas was sick. I did not know yet what I was giving away.

I was nineteen when my grandmother died. At the funeral, my aunt stood up and spoke for several minutes, and the people around me wept at things she said, and I sat in the second row and understood perhaps one word in five. Afterward, a cousin I had met only twice asked me in English whether I had known that my grandmother wrote poems. I had not.

Her notebooks came to me, because I was the eldest grandchild. There are four of them, bound in faded green cloth, and they are filled with her small, slanting handwriting. I have been taking classes for two years now, at a community center on Saturday mornings, sitting among children half my age who correct my tones with great patience. I can read the notebooks slowly, one line at a time, with a dictionary open beside me.

Some of the poems are about the house where she grew up. One is about me. In it, she describes a small girl who answers every question with a shrug, and she writes that she is waiting for the day when the girl will want to talk. I read that poem more often than the others, and each time I wish I could tell her that the day has come.

I have a confession to make: I can no longer find my way to my own dentist. I have been going to the same office for six years, and every time, I type the address into my phone and follow a calm voice that tells me when to turn. Last month the phone died in a parking garage, and I sat in my car for several minutes like a dog that has been told to stay, waiting for instructions that had stopped coming.

This is a little embarrassing, because I grew up in a family of map readers. My father kept a road atlas in the car so worn that the pages for our own state had come loose and were held together by a rubber band. On long drives, my sister and I took turns navigating, and we argued about routes with the passion other families saved for politics.

Researchers who study the brain have suggested that finding our own way exercises the parts of memory that build mental maps, and that people who rely entirely on turn-by-turn directions may let those skills weaken. I cannot judge the science, but I can report my own results. After six years of being guided, I could tell you the name of every song I listened to on the way to the dentist, and very little about the streets I drove down.

So this spring I tried an experiment. Once a week, I leave the phone in the glove compartment and drive somewhere I know only roughly, steering by landmarks and the position of the sun. The first attempt took forty minutes longer than it should have and ended at a car wash I had never seen before, three towns from where I meant to go. I bought a car wash anyway, since I was there.

Things have improved. I can now reach the dentist without help, and I have discovered a hardware store with a parrot in the window, a shortcut along the river that saves four minutes, and a hill from which you can see the whole valley at sunset. My screen would have shown me none of these, since I would have had to ask for them first.

I am under no illusion that I will give up the phone entirely. On a rainy night in a strange city, I will be glad of the calm voice. But I have come to think that being a little lost now and then is good for a person, the way a short walk in the cold is good for a person: unpleasant at the start and clarifying by the end.

For most of the nineteenth century, Mill Creek ran openly through the middle of Harwick, turning the wheels of three gristmills and a woolen factory before emptying into the Sable River. By 1900 the mills had closed, and the creek had become what one newspaper called "the town's longest gutter," carrying runoff from the streets and waste from the houses along its banks.

In 1923 the city council voted to solve the problem by making it disappear. Over the next four years, workers built a brick tunnel along the creek's path, about eight feet high, and diverted the water into it. Above the tunnel they laid soil, then paving, then a broad avenue lined with shops. The council's report called the project "a permanent improvement," and for a generation most residents seemed to agree.

The creek, however, had other ideas. A tunnel built for the flows of the 1920s had to carry far more water as the city grew and the fields upstream were covered with houses and parking lots. In 1958, and again in 1971 and 1989, heavy rains overwhelmed the tunnel, and Mill Creek rose through the storm drains into the basements of the shops above it. Each repair cost more than the one before.

The council of 1923 can hardly be blamed for failing to foresee the size of the modern city. What is harder to excuse is the way the decision was made. The minutes of the council's meetings show that an engineer named Ruth Galloway proposed an alternative: cleaning the creek, widening its channel, and lining it with a park that could flood safely in heavy storms. Her plan was estimated to cost about the same as the tunnel. It was dismissed in a single meeting, after one council member remarked that a park was "no business of a city government."

Today, Harwick is considering opening part of the creek again, a practice that engineers call "daylighting." The cost of removing the tunnel beneath three blocks has been estimated at forty million dollars, many times what Galloway's park would have cost even after a century of rising prices. Supporters point out that an open channel can spread floodwater across its banks, which a tunnel cannot do.

Whatever Harwick decides, the story of Mill Creek is a reminder that the cheapest solution is the one that is cheapest over a hundred years, rather than the one that is quickest to finish. The creek, however, had other ideas. A tunnel built for the flows of the 1920s had to carry far more water as the city grew and the fields upstream were covered with houses and parking lots. In the spring of 2019, a biologist named Priya Raman bolted a small wooden box to a fence post behind her house in the town of Eastmere. The box had a clear plastic front, so that the peanuts inside were plainly visible, and a lid that opened only if a bird pulled a short loop of string and then pushed a sliding latch with its beak. Raman wanted to know whether the crows that visited her yard could learn the sequence, and, if one did, whether the others would learn it from watching.

For eleven days the crows inspected the box from a careful distance. Crows are famously cautious about new objects, and Raman had expected a long wait. On the twelfth day, a young crow she had nicknamed Notch, for a gap in one wing, landed on the post, tugged the string, and pecked at the latch until it slid. The lid swung open. Notch took a peanut and flew to a nearby roof to eat it.

What happened next was the real subject of the study. Over the following three weeks, Raman's cameras recorded every visit to the box. The crows that had watched Notch from the fence opened the box, on average, after nine attempts. Crows that arrived later and had seen no other bird use it needed more than forty attempts, and several gave up entirely.

Raman noticed something else. Several of the watching crows did not copy Notch's exact movements. Notch always pulled the string with a sideways jerk of the head; two of the others learned to hook it with one foot instead. The birds seemed to have learned what needed to happen, the string pulled and the latch pushed, rather than simply repeating a series of motions. It is a remarkably flexible kind of learning for an animal that weighs about a pound.

That distinction matters to scientists, because learning the goal of an action is generally considered a harder mental task than copying the action itself. Raman is careful to say that a single yard and a single box cannot settle the question, and she has since placed boxes in eleven other yards across the region to see whether the pattern holds. Even with those cautions, it is hard to watch the footage of Notch working the latch and see anything but a clever animal solving a problem.

For her part, Raman says the study changed how she looks out her kitchen window. The crows she once thought of as noisy neighbors now seem to her like a small research team of their own, testing every new object she puts out. Last winter, she says, one of them opened the box, took a peanut, and left a bottle cap on the fence post beside it.

When Ada Pruitt died in 1987, her family found more than nine hundred glass jars in the cellar of her farmhouse in the hill country of western Virginia. Each held a handful of dried beans, and each was labeled in pencil with a name, a date, and the family that had given them to her: "Greasy Grits, 1954, from the Mullins family"; "Cut-Short, 1961, Hattie Stallard." Over thirty years, Pruitt had built one of the largest private collections of old bean varieties in the country, and almost nobody outside her county knew it existed.

Pruitt was a schoolteacher by profession. She began collecting after she noticed that the beans her students' grandparents grew were disappearing, replaced by the uniform varieties sold in seed catalogs. The old beans had been saved and passed down within families for generations, each suited to a particular valley or hillside, and when a family stopped planting, its beans could vanish within a single season.

Her method was simple and slow. On weekends and during summers, she drove the back roads in a green pickup truck, stopping at farmhouses to ask whether anyone still grew "the old beans." She never took more than a cupful, and she always left something in return, usually a jar of her own preserves. Then she planted a few seeds of every variety in her garden each year, so that the collection stayed alive rather than aging on a shelf.

Pruitt kept careful records of more than the beans themselves. Her notebooks, which run to forty volumes, record how each family cooked a variety, which ones were prized for drying and which for eating green, and the stories attached to them. One family's bean had supposedly been carried over the mountains in a coat pocket in 1838; another was said to have been the only crop that survived a summer of drought.

After her death, her nephew offered the collection to a university seed bank. Researchers there found that many of Pruitt's varieties existed nowhere else, and several have since been shared with farmers and gardeners across the region. Plant breeders have studied a few of them for their resistance to disease, a trait that the uniform catalog varieties often lack.

It is tempting to describe Pruitt as a keeper of the past, but that description misses what made her work last. She understood that a seed is only safe while someone is planting it, and so she kept her collection in the ground as well as in jars. Her patience, spread over thirty summers and nine hundred jars, saved what a single generation of neglect could have erased.
